channel.description: "Lockhart Nuke Watch" was started to try and gather information about the Groves Isotope nuclear reactor being built in Lockhart, Texas by Oklo. Find us at on Facebook at https://www.facebook.com/groups/987252890512778.

item.title: Groves-1 reaches criticality: what's actually going on at the site
item.content:encoded:
On August 5, 2026, **Groves-1** — Oklo's Groves Isotope Test Reactor in Lockhart — reached initial criticality. Then, on November 11, the DOE [cleared it for unrestricted operations](https://investor.oklo.com/news/news-details/2026/Oklos-Groves-1-to-Begin-Research-and-Demonstration-Phase-after-being-Cleared-by-U-S--Department-of-Energy-for-Unrestricted-Operations/default.aspx), beginning what Oklo describes as a "research and demonstration phase."
A reactor in active operation is a bigger deal for the community than a reactor in commissioning. The most complete independent accounts of what this clearance means are the American Nuclear Society's [Nuclear News roundup from this week](https://www.ans.org/news/2026-11-16/article-8581/oklo-roundup-groves1-plans-centrus-contract-aurora-concrete/) and [World Nuclear News' coverage of the November 11 clearance](https://www.world-nuclear-news.org/articles/us-test-reactor-cleared-for-operations). We dug further into what's actually in the public record about the site itself. (A companion piece covers the separately announced Groves-2 Forge pilot: [Groves-2 Forge: a Lu-177 pilot — but where, and under what review?](/updates/2026-11-16-oklo-groves-2-forge-lu-177/).)
## What the DOE's own environmental document says about Groves-1
The DOE NEPA determination for Groves-1 ([CX-271014](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2026-06/CX-271014.pdf)) is the first real, citable description of the site, published June 15, 2026:
- Maximum power **100 watts**, operating phase of **about 100 hours**, planned complete by end of 2026 - **5 Framatome GAIA fuel assemblies**, low-enriched uranium dioxide, and "the reactor won't be refueled" - A 4,600 sq ft building (1,650 sq ft reactor room) containing a **35-foot-deep, below-grade concrete pool**, on the Proto-Town site in Caldwell County (0.2 mi NW of Mineral Springs Rd, 0.1 mi SW of West Fork Rd), within Oklo's lease of ~47 acres - Maximum hypothetical accident: a fuel-handling accident with cladding failure; DOE says the dose consequences to workers and public are "minimal" - Water: ~180,000–200,000 gal/yr potable, **~35,000 gal/yr pool makeup**, a **100,000-gallon static firewater tank** - Waste: "very small quantities"; **no liquid radioactive sources of concern expected**; contaminated structures shipped to "a commercially operated low-level radioactive waste disposal facility"
Read closely, this document describes a **short-duration, near-zero-power experiment** — not a production plant. It is a categorical exclusion (B5.26) covering *Groves-1 only*, issued for a specific proposed action: fuel possession and operation of that reactor. **Groves-2 is not in it.** The pilot plant Oklo announced on October 13 will need its own DOE authorization and environmental review — and until that document exists, no one, including Oklo's press office, can tell you what the safety basis of Groves-2 actually is. We cover that gap in our [Groves-2 piece](/updates/2026-11-16-oklo-groves-2-forge-lu-177/).
## The construction record doesn't match the environmental review
The state's [TABS record (TABS2026014595)](https://www.tdlr.texas.gov/TABS/Projects/TABS2026014595) for the "Groves" project at Proto Town, 2600 Mineral Springs Rd, lists a **7,600 sq ft** single-story industrial facility, "Inspection Complete" as of April 2026, estimated cost $23M, privately funded. Two things to note: the DOE's own NEPA document describes a **4,600 sq ft** building — and the TABS record names the tenant as **Thomas Eiden**, founder of Atomic Alchemy, the isotope company Oklo acquired in February 2025. Either the building grew after the environmental determination was written, or the footprints describe different scopes. We'd like Oklo to explain.
## There's still no NRC record for the reactor
Searches of [NRC ADAMS](https://www.nrc.gov/reading-rm/adams) for the Groves *reactor* still yield nothing, for the same reason as in our last update: the pilot-phase reactor runs under **DOE authorization, not NRC licensing**. Our [FOIA requests](/topics/00-foia-requests/) are still the main channel for the missing reactor design documents. That will start to change only if and when the commercial track for Groves-2 begins — the licensing path Oklo is counting on, and the new October NRC rule that makes it more plausible, are covered in our [Groves-2 piece](/updates/2026-11-16-oklo-groves-2-forge-lu-177/).
## What the November 11 clearance means
Per [Nuclear News](https://www.ans.org/news/2026-11-16/article-8581/oklo-roundup-groves1-plans-centrus-contract-aurora-concrete/), Groves-1 was the **fifth reactor to reach criticality through DOE's Reactor Pilot Program** (one of 11 projects the DOE selected for it in August 2025), and the November 11 clearance makes it what Oklo describes as an "operating platform for research, testing, and training" — explicitly to test capabilities "relevant to future isotope reactors and Oklo's fast fission reactors, the Aurora Powerhouse."
The work has already begun: during a recent startup, operators wore eye-tracking glasses, with the data to be used to "improve the facility's human-machine interface and inform future design choices."
Per [World Nuclear News](https://www.world-nuclear-news.org/articles/us-test-reactor-cleared-for-operations), the clearance's scope extends beyond Oklo's own roadmap: it includes continued control-rod drive mechanism testing and "criticality and reactivity benchmarking" that Oklo says will help improve fuel performance and power output in **small and large light water reactors** — Groves-1 is, in part, a benchmarking and training asset for the broader light-water fleet, not just a stepping stone for Aurora. Oklo also positions it explicitly as a training and qualification platform for the nuclear personnel who will staff future reactor deployments.
Not every RPP participant keeps its demonstration reactor — fellow participant Antares has fully disassembled its Mark-0. Oklo will keep Groves-1 as an operating research and training facility, presumably for the long term. For the neighborhood, that means a working research reactor is not a temporary experiment: it's a standing presence.
## First responders: still in the dark
And yet the emergency-planning questions from our [May 11 update](/updates/2026-05-11-our-response-to-oklo/) remain unanswered. [Reporting from The Texas Observer, summarized by Magica](https://magica.com/news/oklo-groves-reactor-emergency-planning-lockhart), notes that Oklo **declined to confirm whether it had conducted local emergency drills or would hold a public safety meeting**. That was about a 100-watt test reactor *in commissioning* — now it's operating with unrestricted clearance.
If the announced Groves-2 Forge pilot ever comes to the same backyard, the hazard picture changes entirely — our [Groves-2 piece](/updates/2026-11-16-oklo-groves-2-forge-lu-177/) covers what a continuously operating irradiation facility plus a hot cell of radioactive chemistry would mean for emergency response.
- What is the radiological emergency response plan, and who has it? - Has the fire department been trained — and with what equipment? - Who at the site is available 24/7/365 to brief responders? - What communication protocol do Lockhart residents have, beyond "we will share appropriate public information as the project advances"?
## What we're watching
1. **Status of our FOIA requests** to the DOE — still pending, and still the cleanest path to the reactor design documents Oklo cites as trade secrets. 2. **Emergency planning and first-responder training** — any confirmation of drills, a public safety meeting, or a radiological emergency response plan. The unrestricted-operations clearance makes this more urgent, not less. 3. **What Groves-1 is actually doing** — the cleared work includes control-rod drive testing and reactivity benchmarking. We'll be watching DOE publications and Oklo announcements for what happens inside the reactor next.
Groves-1 started as a modest experiment — 100 watts, a hundred hours, five fuel assemblies, a building whose construction record doesn't quite match its environmental review. Under the latest clearance it becomes a standing research, testing, and training platform: a working reactor in this neighborhood, not a temporary experiment. The name says "Groves." Public records do not really say what happens next.

item.title: Groves-2 Forge: a Lu-177 pilot, but where, and under what review?
item.content:encoded:
Groves-2 Forge is a different category of facility from the 100-watt experiment its name borrows from: a reactor plus a chemical plant, producing material potent enough to treat cancer. The chemistry suggests a megawatt-class machine, on a site whose location, power level, and safety basis the public has not yet seen.
On October 13, 2026, Oklo [announced that it is advancing **Groves-2 Forge**](https://oklo.com/newsroom/oklo-to-advance-groves-2-forge-as-part-of-u-s-department-of-energys-nuclear-energy-launch-pad-se), an "isotope production and processing pilot facility" that will combine reactor irradiation with hot-cell processing: isotope separation, product recovery, packaging and transportation. Production will initially focus on **lutetium-177 (Lu-177)**, a radioisotope used in targeted cancer therapies such as Pluvicto and Lutathera.
This announcement comes on the back of the [DOE's Nuclear Energy Launch Pad](https://inl.gov/news-release/nric-selects-new-nuclear-energy-launch-pad-participants-to-boost-nuclear-energy/) selection on August 24, Groves-1's initial criticality on August 5 and its [clearance for unrestricted operations on November 11](https://investor.oklo.com/news/news-details/2026/Oklos-Groves-1-to-Begin-Research-and-Demonstration-Phase-after-being-Cleared-by-U-S--Department-of-Energy-for-Unrestricted-Operations/default.aspx). What that clearance means for the existing site, including the first citable description of Groves-1 in the DOE's own environmental document, is covered in our [companion piece on Groves-1](/updates/2026-11-16-groves-1-criticality/). A [DiscoveryAlert article](https://discoveryalert.com/news/oklo-lutetium-177-production-october-2026/) explains the motivation for Lu-177 processing and the difference in the DOE "demonstration" vs NRC "commercial" tracks. We also dug further into articles from American Nuclear Society, [Nuclear News roundup from this week](https://www.ans.org/news/2026-11-16/article-8581/oklo-roundup-groves1-plans-centrus-contract-aurora-concrete/), [coverage of the October 13 announcement](https://www.ans.org/news/2026-10-15/article-8492/oklo-announces-plans-for-groves2/), plus [World Nuclear News' report on the November 11 clearance](https://www.world-nuclear-news.org/articles/us-test-reactor-cleared-for-operations). All of them fill in several of the gaps below.
> "Groves showed how quickly a new reactor could be built and brought to criticality through close collaboration between the private sector and DOE. Groves-2 Forge will build directly on that foundation by adding the capabilities needed to irradiate target materials and process and prepare valuable isotopes." — Jacob DeWitte, Oklo cofounder and CEO, to *Nuclear News*
Ok, so we have a general idea of what Groves-2 Forge might do...
## Where will Groves-2 Forge _actually be_?
**None of announcements say!** They describe the facility, the program, and the isotope, but not a location. On the [November 6 Q3 earnings call](https://www.watchlistnews.com/oklo-q3-earnings-call-highlights/11300258.html), Oklo management said the Groves-2 facility "site is **still being finalized**," and listed "starting Groves-2 construction" as a future target "dependent on execution and required approvals."
In its [Fall 2026 Groves Teach-in deck](https://s203.q4cdn.com/103172959/files/doc_presentations/2026/Sep/30/Fall-2026-Groves-Teach-in-vF.pdf), Oklo describes its deployment playbook as "local permits and community engagement as **step one**". The language strongly suggests no site is locked in. That matters because the Launch Pad program launched in March 2026 as the successor to DOE's 2025 Reactor Pilot Program, which NRIC has now filled with two rounds of selections (four companies, then eight) has two pathways: one at [Idaho National Laboratory](https://nric.inl.gov/nuclear-energy-launch-pad-at-idaho-national-laboratory/), and "Launch Pad USA," which extends the framework to **non-federal sites anywhere in the country**.
So on the current record, Groves-2 Forge could be:
- an expansion of the existing 47-acre Oklo lease at Proto-Town in Caldwell County, - a brand new site in Texas or elsewhere, or - a facility at INL in Idaho wearing a "Groves" name for marketing continuity.
And here's the pressure point: the same Q3 company update, as reported by [Nuclear News](https://www.ans.org/news/2026-11-16/article-8581/oklo-roundup-groves1-plans-centrus-contract-aurora-concrete/), says Oklo plans to **begin construction of Groves-2 Forge within the next 12 months**. That's a pretty tight construction timeline for a production isotope facility at an unannounced site! The company also told *Nuclear News* it intends to move Groves-2 from pilot operations to commercial scale "with the appropriate [NRC] licenses for commercial operation" without a word on what that transition actually involves. If the company is serious about that 12-month window, the site question is urgent: **_**the public may only discover where Groves-2 Forge is, if it ends up in Texas, from a TDLR TABS filing rather than from any announcement**.
[The Inference](https://theinference.org/article/oklo-s-cancer-isotope-plant-lands-with-no-buyer-no-price-and-a-6-5-billion-bill) already calls Groves-2 a "Texas pilot plant." Is this speculation on their part, or a hint of what's coming to 'town?
**If a second reactor plus a chemical processing plant is coming to the same backyard in Lockhart, residents should know before the ground breaks, not after.** Texas construction is publicly registered with the state; a new [TDLR TABS](https://www.tdlr.texas.gov/TABS/) entry for the Proto-Town site would be the tell. The site's only current registration, the Groves-1 building, is [broken down in our companion piece](/updates/2026-11-16-groves-1-criticality/).
We'll be watching!
## What's in the open record about Groves-2
**1. There is no DOE environmental review for Groves-2 yet.** The [DOE NEPA determination for Groves-1 (CX-271014)](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2026-06/CX-271014.pdf) covers *Groves-1 only*: a categorical exclusion (B5.26) issued for fuel possession and operation of that one reactor. A production pilot with its own reactor, irradiation positions, and a hot cell will need its own DOE authorization and environmental review. Groves-1's was [published on energy.gov](https://www.energy.gov/nepa/articles/cx-271014-groves-1-project); Groves-2's should appear the same way. Until that document exists, no one, including Oklo's press office, can tell you what the safety basis of Groves-2 actually is. (How modest the Groves-1 document is: 100 watts, a hundred hours, "the reactor won't be refueled", and how the site's construction record complicates it, are [detailed in our companion piece](/updates/2026-11-16-groves-1-criticality/).)
**2. NRC status.** Searches of [NRC ADAMS](https://www.nrc.gov/reading-rm/adams) for the Groves *reactor* still yield nothing, for the same reason as before: the pilot-phase reactor runs under **DOE authorization, not NRC licensing**. The only NRC action so far is the [March 2026 materials license](https://investor.oklo.com/news/news-details/2026/Oklos-Atomic-Alchemy-Granted-U-S--Nuclear-Regulatory-Commission-License-for-Isotope-Material/default.aspx) authorizing isotope handling in Idaho, not Texas. Commercial-scale operation of Groves-2 would eventually require NRC licenses, but Oklo has given no timeline and no docket. **One development that makes that bridge more plausible:** in October, the NRC finalized a rule allowing license applicants to use analyses, test data, and other information from **DOE or Department of [Defense] reactor demonstration programs** in support of commercial reactor license applications ([World Nuclear News](https://www.world-nuclear-news.org/articles/us-test-reactor-cleared-for-operations). That looks like exactly the regulatory path Oklo is counting on for its stated plan to move Groves-2 from DOE-authorized pilot operation to NRC-licensed commercial operation: data earned under DOE authorization counting toward the commercial application. It makes the two-track story more credible, but it is not itself a license, and it produces no public docket or comment period until Oklo actually files.
**3. TCEQ and DSHS searches reveal nothing on Groves-2 yet.** We searched every publicly queryable TCEQ record set: water-quality permits (active and pending, via [data.texas.gov](https://data.texas.gov/)), the pending NSR and Title V air-permit lists, [pending radioactive-material license applications](https://www.tceq.texas.gov/permitting/radmat/radmat-pending-license-apps), and the hazardous-waste registration and annual-report datasets. Zero results for Oklo, Atomic Alchemy, Mineral Springs Frontier, Proto Town, or Eiden. [TDLR TABS](https://www.tdlr.texas.gov/TABS/) shows exactly one registration for the site: the Groves-1 building above. No "Groves-2" appears in any of them. A TCEQ [Permit Search](https://permit-search.tceq.texas.gov/) only shows [a stormwater permit for Proto-Town](https://permit-search.tceq.texas.gov/PermitViewResult?addnId=970513152025225&mapTypeId=roadmap&lt=l&r=15&pId=ChIJ-zyRzgNRQ4YRh6l-eDM-Wkw&lat=29.7986218&lng=-97.654811&ps=na|ip|ra&mp=ai:ans,ao|ws:apor,ccr,dcr,ec,cocml,iahw,ica,mswd,mswp,pst,ur,rwd,rwsp,pstsi,ti,uic,uo,asvs|wt:agpor,ea,ossf,pws,st,wqp,wrr,waa,wa,sl). The Department of State Health Services (DSHS) is the primary state licensing authority over **possession, use, and storage** of [radioactive material in Texas](https://www.dshs.texas.gov/texas-radiation-control/radioactive-material-licensing-radiation-control-program). DSHS's Radiation Control Program regulates byproduct material of exactly the kind a Lu-177 plant would handle. TCEQ's jurisdiction is mostly downstream, at the disposal end. We'll be watching DSHS's license roster alongside TCEQ's databases.
**4. What Oklo's own deck reveals.** The [teach-in presentation](https://s203.q4cdn.com/103172959/files/doc_presentations/2026/Sep/30/Fall-2026-Groves-Teach-in-vF.pdf) shows the commercial isotope production reactor: "compact," "multiple reactors per facility," 100% capacity allocated to isotope production, still marked **"WORKING DRAFT."** It also names the isotope pipeline beyond Lu-177: **Tb-161** (from Gd-160 targets), **Pb-212** via a thorium generator ("Oklo route"), and **I-131**. Each of those is a different target chemistry and a different waste profile.
## How Lu-177 is made
Oklo has already disclosed its target feedstock: in September it announced receiving [two grams of enriched ytterbium-176](https://oklo.com/blog/two-grams-to-help-build-americas-isotope-supply) from Actinide Inc., "a stable isotope that with the addition of a single neutron in a nuclear reactor yields Lu-177."
There are [two reactor routes](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4463871/#Sec3:~:text=177Lu%20Production%20Process):
| Route | Reaction | Product | |---|---|---| | Direct | ¹⁷⁶Lu(n,γ)¹⁷⁷Lu | **Carrier-added** Lu-177 mixed with Lu-177m| | Indirect | ¹⁷⁶Yb(n,γ)¹⁷⁷Yb → β⁻ → ¹⁷⁷Lu | **No-carrier-added** pure Lu-177, the form preferred for drug labeling |
Oklo's Yb-176 feedstock means the **indirect route**: neutrons turn Yb-176 into Yb-177 (half-life 1.9 hours), which beta-decays into Lu-177 (half-life 6.65 days). Chemists then separate the lutetium from the bulk ytterbium. The "no-carrier-added" quality is what makes it valuable for radiopharmaceuticals. The product from the indirect route is not tainted with a longer-lasting Lu-177m isotope.
What this chemistry means for a site:
- **The process input is valuable ytterbium.** Recovering and recycling the enriched Yb-176 is a core part of the process (Yb-176 is expensive and globally scarce; DeWitte's blog post jokes that every isotope company "has access to 200 grams of ytterbium" from the same Russian stockpile). - **Ytterbium and lutetium are neighboring lanthanides — chemically almost twins.** Separating them takes repeated extraction steps, which means a hot cell running extraction chemistry: acids, resins, solvent, filters, and gloves. **That process waste is low-level radioactive**, and it's the ordinary daily output of any Lu-177 plant. Groves-1, running 100 watts for 100 hours, was certified as a *Very Small Quantity Generator* of hazardous waste under RCRA/TCEQ with "very small quantities" of radioactive waste ([details](/updates/2026-11-16-groves-1-criticality/)). **A processing facility is a different animal.** What will Groves-2's waste generator classification be? Where do the liquid and solid waste streams go? Texas's rules give a concrete menu of answers, and we've pulled TCEQ's own [RG-486 guide on radioactive material exemptions](/assets/pdf/rg-486-radioactive-material-exemptions.pdf) into the record:
- Waste that meets the rule's criteria is **"exempt by rule"** from radioactive-waste disposal requirements and can go to an ordinary or hazardous-waste landfill instead of a licensed low-level waste facility. Disposal facilities routinely require a TCEQ **"exemption concurrence"** letter before accepting such a shipment; requests are free, go to TCEQ's Radioactive Materials Division, and typically take about two weeks. That's a concrete, checkable paper trail to look for later. - Texas **prohibits dilution** to lower a waste's classification (30 TAC 336.229), and containers can't be averaged together to pass the limits: each container is characterized on its own. So "just dilute it" is not an option, but every decayed process stream still gets classified individually.
Read together, the ordinary, short-lived output of a Lu-177 plant: resins, filters, gloves and decayed product could plausibly end up at a regional landfill with an exemption concurrence in the file, never touching a licensed low-level waste facility. This means the endpoint of this facility's everyday waste could be a local solid-waste facility, and the people living around it would want to know. Which facility? Which waste streams? Oklo has not said.
- **The product itself is a high-activity beta emitter.** Lu-177 emits betas up to 497 keV (mean ~134 keV) and low-energy gammas at 113 keV (10.4%) and 208 keV (6.4%). Shielding a vial is easy; shielding a pilot production line processing grams of material at clinical strength is an engineering question the public has not yet seen answered. And with a 6.65-day half-life, product (and waste) decays on a timescale that forces continuous make-and-ship operations. - **The reactor's coolant will be activated.** Any pool-type reactor produces trace activation in its water, including [tritium](/archive/20-waste-tritium/). The Groves-1 determination waved this away as negligible for 100 watts and a hundred hours, not extrapolatable to a production reactor whose power level **has not been disclosed**. The commercial reactor in Oklo's deck is a "working draft." What is the thermal power of the Groves-2 pilot reactor? That single number drives the decay heat, the cooling requirements, the fission-product inventory in the fuel, and the size of the emergency planning zone. Oklo has not said, but the chemistry gives us a way to estimate it. - **Spent fuel.** Groves-1's five GAIA assemblies were designed never to be refueled ([companion piece](/updates/2026-11-16-groves-1-criticality/)). Groves-2 will be refueled, on a schedule Oklo hasn't published. The Groves-1 NEPA describes interim storage in the reactor tank before shipment to licensed facilities or "Oklo's planned fuel recycling facility." Where does Groves-2's spent fuel sit, for how long, and under whose oversight?
## What kind of reactor does this chemistry actually demand?
Oklo has not disclosed the Forge reactor's power. But the Lu-177 math is public, and every facility in the world that actually runs it is on the record.
**The production rate scales directly with neutron flux.** The Yb-176(n,γ) reaction has a small thermal capture cross section (about 3.1 barns) so the only way to make useful quantities is to push a very large number of neutrons through the target. The result, per a 2021 review in the *European Journal of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging*: "Current production of ¹⁷⁷Lu, both for carrier added and no carrier added ¹⁷⁷Lu, is done in reactors with a high neutron flux": BR2 (Belgium), FRM-II (Germany), HFR (Netherlands), IVV-2M (Russia), LVR-15 (Czech Republic), Maria (Poland), MURR (USA), OPAL (Australia), Safari (South Africa), and SM-3 (Russia). Facilities that, the review notes, "have been designed specifically to generate high [fluxes]." Of the three whose specifications are public, all are pool-type research reactors in the **ten-to-twenty-megawatt class**: [MURR in Missouri](https://www.insidehighered.com/news/faculty/research/2025/08/21/u-missouri-forges-ahead-ambitious-nuclear-project), the only reported end-to-end domestic NCA Lu-177 producer, runs a **10 MW** core; [FRM-II in Garching, Germany](https://mediatum.ub.tum.de/id/1080831) runs **20 MW**; and [OPAL in Australia](https://ansto.com/facilities/opal-multi-purpose-reactor) is a **20 MW** multi-purpose reactor.
**The best-documented case of Oklo's exact route is FRM-II.** A Technische Universität München radiochemistry group ran the Yb-176 indirect route there in cooperation with the commercial isotope producer ITG: at a thermal flux of ~1.3×10¹⁴ n/cm²/s, a 100 mg target of 99.7%-enriched Yb-176 yields up to ~94 GBq of NCA Lu-177 over a 14-day irradiation, and targets up to 150 mg produced up to **120 GBq (~3.2 Ci) per cycle**. For scale, a typical patient dose of Lu-177 is 7–9 GBq: one two-week cycle of a 20 MW research reactor makes on the order of a few hundred patient doses. That is the actual tempo of this chemistry.
**Now run the numbers against what Oklo has disclosed:**
- **Two grams of feedstock.** Oklo's entire disclosed Yb-176 inventory is two grams. At FRM-II-like yields, that works out to roughly **1.5 TBq (~40 Ci) per cycle: a few hundred patient doses.** Commercial NCA Lu-177 production runs on kilograms of enriched Yb-176 per year. Two grams is a pilot quantity. - **100 watts vs. 10–20 megawatts.** Groves-1 is capped at 100 watts by its own DOE determination. Neutron flux scales roughly with reactor power: FRM-II's 20 MW produces ~10¹⁴ n/cm²/s, so scaling down 200,000-fold, 100 watts lands near ~10⁹ n/cm²/s: roughly **five orders of magnitude below the flux band where this chemistry produces anything useful**. (Even the simpler carrier-added route, which skips the Yb/Lu separation, is "typically produced at nuclear reactors with intermediate neutron flux of 1–3×10¹⁴ n/cm²/s," per the FRM-II documentation.) No watt-scale reactor gets there.
What the chemistry and the public record seem to imply: **if Groves-2 Forge is what Oklo describes, it contains a reactor at least two to five orders of magnitude larger than Groves-1: a megawatt-class, high-flux machine, more like a small research reactor than a scaled-up test reactor.** The public has not seen that design. The pilot reactor's power, fuel, and cooling have not been published, and the commercial reactor in Oklo's own deck is still a "working draft." That is precisely what the pending DOE NEPA determination for Groves-2 should say. If it describes something far smaller, the question will be how much Lu-177 it can actually make?
The speculative scale needed here is similar to that of Oklo's prior NRC-rejected [VIPR reactor](/archive/10-vipr-reactor) projects.
## The business reality check
The business picture, for what it's worth, cuts both ways: Oklo is also signing long-dated hardware commitments, like its "strategic manufacturing agreement" with U.S. Forged Rings covering **27 Aurora module-equivalents reserved across 2030–2035** (first deliveries 2030). That's a decade-long roadmap written in contracts, on the same equity-financed foundation as everything else. The press release names **no buyer, no price, no production volume, and no federal funding** ([The Inference](https://theinference.org/article/oklo-s-cancer-isotope-plant-lands-with-no-buyer-no-price-and-a-6-5-billion-bill)). The company's own guidance, as covered by [DiscoveryAlert](https://discoveryalert.com/news/oklo-lutetium-177-production-october-2026/) and in its [Q3 2026 results](https://investor.oklo.com/news/news-details/2026/Oklo-Publishes-Third-Quarter-2026-Financial-Results-and-Business-Update/default.aspx), points the first isotope revenue to **early 2027, from the NRC-licensed Idaho laboratory, not from Texas**. Groves-1 cost roughly $65M plus ~$10M in fuel, per management on the Q3 call.
The demand story is real: Novartis's Lu-177 drugs sold roughly $2.8B combined in 2025, with Pluvicto growing 43% in Q2. But "shortage" does not mean "empty field" — the [DiscoveryAlert piece's supplier table](https://discoveryalert.com/news/oklo-lutetium-177-production-october-2026/) (MURR, SHINE, ITM/Eckert & Ziegler, and others) shows a crowded race to fill it, and the University of Missouri Research Reactor remains the only reported end-to-end domestic NCA producer. Meanwhile Oklo reported a **$123.3M net loss** for the first nine months of 2026, funded by $2.3B in at-the-market stock sales: the same equity that built Groves-1.
And note the scale gap we quantified [above](#what-reactor-does-this-chemistry-actually-demand): Oklo's entire disclosed Yb-176 inventory so far is **two grams**. It also tells you this supply chain is at an early stage, with domestic enrichment from Actinide not yet proven at scale.
## What we're watching
1. **Site selection for Groves-2**: any new TABS entry at Proto-Town (or elsewhere), and any announcement. Oklo says it plans to begin construction within 12 months, so the window is now. 2. **The DOE NEPA determination for Groves-2**: it will be the first public statement of the pilot reactor's power, fuel, cooling, accident analysis, and waste. Based on the Lu-177 math above, we expect it to describe a machine far larger than the 100-watt Groves-1; if it doesn't, the question is how much isotope it can actually make. 3. **NRC filings** when the commercial track begins: a Part 52 license and materials licensing, with the usual public comment period. Expect Oklo to invoke the new October rule to fold in its DOE pilot-program data. 4. **TCEQ permits** for any change in waste generator status or process discharges — check TCEQ's new [Permit Search Portal](https://permit-search.tceq.texas.gov/) monthly, since it's the only place post–August 31 applications appear, and the [CID](https://www14.tceq.texas.gov/epic/eCID/) for anything pending before the Commission. Also watch **DSHS** licensing for the processing facility, and TCEQ **exemption concurrences** once waste characterization begins. 5. **Status of our FOIA requests** to the DOE are still pending.

item.title: What is the Groves reactor? A dubious experiment?
item.content:encoded:
Oklo released a [Texas fact sheet](/assets/pdf/Oklo-Texas-Q-A.pdf) in response to questions Lockhart Nuke Watch asked about the Preliminary Documented Safety Analysis (PDSA) for the Groves site Oklo is building in Lockhart.
The most significant takeaway: Oklo confirms that Groves will not be a [VIPR reactor](https://www.trtr.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/4-Eiden-Overview-of-the-Versatile-Isotope-Production-Reactor-VIPR.pdf). So the prior analysis on this site, which was based on VIPR (the best guess available from public open sources at the time) is not _immediately_ applicable to Groves. That analysis is still [archived](/archive). It may be useful to other communities who _are_ getting a VIPR.
So if Groves isn't a VIPR... what exactly is it?
That's the purpose of our FOIA requests. Lockhart Nuke Watch wants our community to know what exactly is being built here, because Oklo isn't saying what it is at all... just what it isn't:
## What Groves isn't
- It's not a power reactor. - It's not a VIPR (commercial scale isotope reactor).
The key phrase in the press release: "being developed to build operating experience for future isotope production systems"
So add to that list of what it isn't:
- It's not commercially viable - It's not producing "life-saving cancer therapies"
Reading between the lines of corporate press release-ese, the Texas Q&A leads some group members to conclude that __Groves is a science experiment__. It uses __real uranium nuclear fuel__ in __some unknown quantity__ which will produce some __unknown amount of thermal energy that needs to be dissipated__ and some __unknown amount and types of waste products__ in a __pool of water__ (that goes where?).
These unknowns are why Lockhart Nuke Watch has submitted FOIA requests to the NRC and DOE.
## What Groves appears to be
Groves appears to be an expensive proof-of-concept demonstration. [Analysts suggest](https://www.trefis.com/stock/oklo/articles/599242/oklo-the-25-stock-that-hit-193-and-then-lost-most-of-it/2026-05-13) it is desperately needed to prop up the valuation of Oklo stock with investors by hitting an arbitrary criticality date of July 4, 2026.
As far as can be discerned from public disclosures, __Oklo has yet to produce a single dollar of revenue in 2026__. Not profit, mind you. Revenue. Normally a quarterly report mentions P&L (Profit and Loss). Oklo is only taking the L here. This is a startup that is hurling towards the end of their runway of cash.
Another science experiment doesn't seem likely to actually move the needle on that. In fact, it [isn't going so well for Oklo right now](https://www.investing.com/news/transcripts/earnings-call-transcript-oklo-inc-reports-q1-2026-results-shares-drop-93CH-4682884).
## Will Lockhart be left holding the bag (of dirty water)?
Lockhart Nuke Watch asks, is this a ploy to lure investors, until Oklo turns a profit? That's the big tech startup world. The problem here is they seem to be making it at Lockhart's expense.
Let's be clear about what _really_ matters here: our land, our water and our future.
As far as Oklo's claims of supporting the local community, Lockhart Nuke Watch views the outcome may end up something like this: Oklo manages to lure investors until they see a profit -- the area doesn't see much in the way of jobs or benefit.
Lockhart is left with a radioactive pool of water from a demonstration spark intended to keep the money flowing just a little bit longer.
## It's not over
With a nuclear facility built, Oklo would need to go through another approval process to use the site for other purposes. Oklo hasn't ruled this out. This could become a backdoor for more nuclear activity needing review and oversight.
Oklo hasn't revealed their intentions for the site after they get their Fourth-of-July spark in a tank. Without clear disclosure of health and safety protocols, this creates anxiety within the local area about how a nuclear accident will be handled.
One cannot imagine that Oklo would sink $20M into a site and that would be the end of it.
So, what's next?
Will a site built out for an experiment suddenly pivot to something it wasn't designed or built to specification for? Will Lockhart even be informed?

item.title: Oklo responds with a press release, raising more questions
item.content:encoded:
On May 11, 2026, Oklo seems to have responded to the questions raised by Lockhart Nuke Watch, with a slick press release. They've added a [Texas](https://oklo.com/isotopes/texas/default.aspx) page.
It's very high level and general, and still leaves many questions unanswered. Still, it is at least the start of what is hopefully a dialogue and a commitment to honest transparency with the lives of central Texans at stake.
Oklo's response is below. It raises more questions, which are included inline. As always, readers are encouraged to add their own.
> “Groves: Groves is a pool-type, water-cooled, non-pressurized isotope production reactor using low-enriched uranium fuel. It is connected to Oklo Isotopes’ production technology, with Groves serving as a platform to build operating experience and support future production-scale deployments.
This is consistent with the VIPR materials that have been found from open sources such as the NRC ADAMS website on Atomic Alchemy's prior cancelled projects.
Oklo, can you confirm that this Groves reactor is the same VIPR design, with the same specifications? If not, what are the differences, and where is the NRC documentation for Groves?
Why is the normally open and public documentation on Groves [being completely withheld](/topics/00-foia-requests/#why-were-foia-requests-filed-for-the-groves-site) from the public?
> Oversight: The project is being developed under the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE’s) Reactor Pilot Program (RPP). DOE is the federal authorization authority for this research, development, and demonstration project. Before startup, the project must complete DOE safety reviews, including safety analysis and readiness review steps. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) also monitors RPP projects, and future commercial deployments would go through the NRC’s commercial licensing process. State and local authorities are involved, where applicable, for non-nuclear matters such as construction, emergency coordination, environmental permits, and local compliance.
Where can the central Texas community learn more about the outcome from these DOE safety reviews? Where are they being published?
Has the [Texas Commission on Environmental Quality](https://www.tceq.texas.gov/) assessed this project for environmental impacts? Given the potential for water contamination (see [Tritium](/archive/20-waste-tritium/) for example) in the community, this seems well within TCEQ jurisdiction.
Has the facility passed fire code inspection? What codes were evaluated?
Is the local fire department equipped to safely handle a fire potentially involving radioactive materials?
What other state and local jurisdictions are involved?
What does "where applicable" mean? It could mean that you think none are applicable. Please be specific.
> Fuel: Groves uses low-enriched uranium, or LEU, which is a fuel that is manufactured in the United States and has been used for decades in large commercial reactors around the country. Nuclear fuel is subject to strict nuclear safeguards and security requirements. That includes material control and accounting, physical protection and secure transportation.
> Waste: The Groves site is not being developed as a long-term waste disposal facility. Materials, including spent fuel from the project, will be managed under approved safety and waste-management procedures. That means material is characterized, packaged, stored, transported, and disposed of through federally regulated channels. Any used fuel from Groves is initially stored within the reactor system and adjacent facility structures, where it is passively cooled and safely contained. It will then be transferred to another Oklo site.
How much waste is produced, what kinds of waste, and in what volumes?
How is the local environment protected from becoming contaminated with this waste?
> Business model: The purpose of Groves is to help establish a dependable domestic isotope supply chain. Many critical isotopes are currently produced overseas or in aging facilities. Groves is intended to help validate systems, operating procedures, and production methods that can support future commercial isotope production in the United States.
If Oklo closes this line of business, runs out of funds, etc. how will the site be [decommissioned](https://www.nrc.gov/reading-rm/doc-collections/fact-sheets/decommissioning), and what does that process look like for Lockhart? What would the timeline be like?
> Water use: Groves is not a commercial power plant and is not designed around large-scale steam generation or evaporative cooling. All water is used inside controlled reactor systems for cooling and shielding. Water use, wastewater handling, stormwater management, and any applicable construction or operating permits would be addressed through the appropriate local, state, and federal processes. DOE’s reactor authorization process is intended to ensure authorized facilities protect workers, the public, and the environment.
While it's good to know that this will not be a classic steam pressure reactor, there are still risks with operating a controlled fission reaction.
Given the recent changes to DOE regulations in this capacity, the central Texas community has concerns that this may not be a standard that protects workers, the public or the environment. There are now a lot of "MAY" where there used to be "MUST" language. [See for yourself](https://www.npr.org/2026/01/28/nx-s1-5677187/nuclear-safety-rules-rewritten-trump).
How is the integrity of the light water pool and the heavy water (DANK) tank maintained in the event of problems during [significant transients](/archive/50-significant-reactor-events/#what-happens-if-the-target-material-becomes-stuck-or-jammed-in-the-reactor-how-is-this-handled)
> Safety: Groves is not designed around high-pressure steam generation. As a pool-type, water-cooled, non-pressurized isotope production reactor using low-enriched uranium fuel, Groves uses water in a controlled pool environment for cooling and shielding rather than operating like a large, pressurized commercial power reactor. A “meltdown”, in technical terms, is what happens if the fuel is damaged, cooling is lost, or radioactive material is released. The DOE safety review will analyze credible accident scenarios, including fuel damage and release pathways, and it will define barriers, operating limits, monitoring, and emergency actions required before startup. > > The design accounts for material stress, component reliability, seismic and natural-hazard conditions, mechanical failures, and off-normal events. Under DOE’s Reactor Pilot Program authorization process, those issues are addressed through the project’s safety basis, including hazard analysis, accident analysis, safety-classified structures, operating limits, and DOE review before startup.
Why are these reviews being withheld from public review and comment? Where can the public review them?
What kind of testing has been done to assure the public that this site is actually safe?
Has a reactor of this design ever been operated under the conditions and parameters proposed here?
Will there be regular testing of the surrounding air and water to detect contamination leaks?
> Emergency response: Offsite protective actions, if they are deemed necessary, would be coordinated with all the appropriate federal, state, and local emergency-management authorities. At Oklo, we are committed to working with Caldwell County officials and will share appropriate public information on emergency planning as the project advances. Residents should expect clear information on who is responsible, how notifications would occur, and what protective actions, if any, are required.
Are there 24-7 Oklo staff _onsite_ ready to respond to a reactor incident, should one occur?
It is difficult to understand the meaning of "offsite protective actions" here. Hopefully it means Oklo is going to work with local first responders in person -- and not phone in a cleanup request remotely!
Given this reactor is planned to go critical in July 2026, have local first responders received the necessary training to respond to incidents involving the reactor?
Given that the communication plan is still being worked out, when will there be an update on what to expect, and how will this be delivered to the community? How does this work at Oklo's other sites? For a July 2026 target date, this is rapidly approaching.
What kinds of regular audits will be done to ensure the site remains in compliance?
> Proto-Town partnership: Groves is an isotope production project. It is not a weapons project, and Oklo does not design or manufacture weapons. The Groves facility is being developed to support domestic isotope production for uses such as cancer diagnosis and treatment, advanced manufacturing, scientific research, space applications, and national security needs. Other Proto-Town tenants are separate companies with separate businesses. Any site-level relationships should not be confused with a technical partnership or shared mission.
The main concern here is transparency, due diligence and the safety of the community in the surrounding area.
Can you elaborate on the meaning and consequences of isotopes for "space applications" and "national security needs" at all?
> Power vs isotopes: Oklo’s business model includes three main business lines: power, fuel, and isotopes. Groves is part of Oklo’s isotope business line and its purpose is to gather operating experience, validate systems and procedures, and support future commercial isotope production in the United States.”
Does Oklo have plans to bring these other lines of business to central Texas? Is this paving the way for even more projects in the area?
> Please let us know if our office can be of further assistance with this matter.
